findings.source_passage: His acquaintances resented the fact that he turned up in popular cafés with her and, leaving her at a table, sauntered about, chatting with whomsoever he knew. Though I was curious to see her, I had no desire to meet her—but I did.
findings.source_locator: paragraph after 'The fact that he had one was insisted upon wherever he was known.'
findings.why_it_matters: This is voice-establishing Nick — the hedged curiosity, the ironic social observation of Tom's café behaviour. Cutting it removes Nick's characteristic moral register and the detail that Tom flaunts Myrtle publicly, which frames the chapter.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the two sentences about acquaintances resenting Tom's café behaviour and Nick's 'curious to see her...but I did' hedge.

findings.source_passage: The man peered doubtfully into the basket... 'It's more of an Airedale.' He passed his hand over the brown washrag of a back. 'Look at that coat. Some coat. That's a dog that'll never bother you with catching cold.'
findings.why_it_matters: The dog-seller's patter ('brown washrag of a back,' 'never bother you with catching cold') is a comic set-piece of period street voice. The draft collapses it into narration ('After some dispute...'), erasing the texture the plan flagged as essential comic material.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore at least the 'brown washrag of a back' / 'never bother you with catching cold' beat and the seller's direct speech to preserve the tonal comedy.

findings.source_passage: 'I told that boy about the ice.' Myrtle raised her eyebrows in despair at the shiftlessness of the lower orders. 'These people! You have to keep after them all the time.'
findings.source_locator: after Tom tells Myrtle to get ice
findings.why_it_matters: This is the sharpest instance of the 'vitality-to-hauteur' transformation the plan explicitly says to preserve — Myrtle's class performance rendered in Nick's most cuttingly ironic free-indirect voice ('shiftlessness of the lower orders'). Its loss guts the satirical arc of the party.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the ice/'These people!' beat with Nick's 'shiftlessness of the lower orders' gloss intact.

findings.source_passage: 'I married him because I thought he was a gentleman,' she said finally. 'I thought he knew something about breeding, but he wasn't fit to lick my shoe.'
findings.source_locator: Myrtle's explanation of her marriage to Wilson
findings.why_it_matters: Myrtle's 'gentleman'/'breeding'/'lick my shoe' line is one of the chapter's most-quoted character-defining speeches — it is the interpretive key to Myrtle's class aspiration and her contempt for Wilson. Cutting it leaves her motivation opaque.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the 'gentleman / breeding / not fit to lick my shoe' speech and the 'Crazy about him!' exchange that follows.

findings.source_passage: The late afternoon sky bloomed in the window for a moment like the blue honey of the Mediterranean—then the shrill voice of Mrs. McKee called me back into the room.
findings.source_locator: transition between Catherine's Monte Carlo speech and Mrs. McKee's 'kike' speech
findings.why_it_matters: 'Blue honey of the Mediterranean' is a distinctive Fitzgerald lyric image that punctuates the squalor with a sudden aesthetic lift — a small but signature cadence.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the 'blue honey of the Mediterranean' sentence as the transition.

summary: Valley-of-ashes and nose-breaking signatures land, but the draft loses Myrtle's 'lower orders' hauteur beat, her 'gentleman/breeding' speech, the dog-seller's patter, and the 'blue honey of the Mediterranean' lyric — four voice/signature losses across the compressed middle.
